policy: This is the single source for composite assembly recognition, duplicate-child suppression, and assembled-instance swaps. Cycle 02 recorded the six hard-coded renderer branches verbatim. Cycle 05 replaced them: src/equipment/composites.ts evaluates this file, src/player/EquipmentView.tsx asks that module for an asset override, a suppression decision, and an overlay, and src/runtime/reducer.ts asks it to resolve an instance swap. Neither file names an apparatus.
invariants: A composite parent must not also declare state assets. A state asset wins the asset override but does not suppress child rendering, so the parent would render its state art while the child stays hidden — an assembly missing a part. No composite parent has state assets today; the checker keeps it that way and src/equipment/composites.ts makes the precedence explicit instead of accidental.

Every composite must name its participants with a role, the snap zone each non-parent participant must occupy, its result asset, the participants it suppresses, and its detach, recovery, and reset behaviour.
A nested participant names attachmentParentRole so its snap zone is validated against the participant that actually owns it rather than against the composite root.
Suppression may name only declared participants, so a composite can never hide equipment that is not part of it.

A visual composite is recognised passively and re-derived from live attachments on every render, so detaching a participant restores both the parent's base art and the participant's own art with no extra bookkeeping.

An instance-swap composite is the only kind that mutates runtime state. It must declare the learner-facing message and recovery used when the swap cannot proceed, because that text is no longer allowed to live in the reducer.

kinds.visual: The participants stay separate runtime instances. The parent layer renders resultAsset and every suppressed participant stops drawing its own art. Nothing in runtime state changes.
kinds.instance-swap: The participants leave the bench and one assembled instance takes their place. The reducer owns the swap; the renderer only ever sees the assembled definition.
